name: c-blosc2 (Blosc2 shuffle+lz4)
baseline: memcpy (uncompressed copy); inner codecs lz4/zstd/zlib are components, not rivals
workload: Repo bench suite (bench/b2bench.c) on 4 MiB synthetic 32-bit data with 19 significant bits, shuffle filter plus LZ4 codec, 256 MB working set, 8 threads: compressed-chunk read and write versus plain memcpy of the same buffer.
claimed_speedup: At 8 threads, lz4+shuffle clevel 1 (ratio 4.75): decompression 31337.5 MB/s vs memcpy(read) 8962.2 MB/s, and compression 13172.7 MB/s vs memcpy(write) 9641.2 MB/s (derived from page data: about 3.5x on decode and 1.4x on encode). Same file at 16 threads: decomp 35428.1 MB/s vs memcpy read 9311.2 MB/s. Single thread decode (5293.7 MB/s) is slower than memcpy (8581.6 MB/s).
hardware: Host named only 'corex' in the output (CPU model not stated)
stars_or_usage: 586 stars; used by PyTables, h5py, Zarr per README
tradeoffs: Meta-compressor: needs typed, regular binary data (shuffle/bitshuffle filters) to win; gains come from multithreading and cache effects; chunked frame format and NDim layer add API surface.
caveats: Result file is from Blosc 2.0.0.beta.6 (2020) with LZ4 1.9.3 and Zstd 1.4.9; CPU model and compiler flags are not stated, so only partial methodology (first-party, tier C). Baseline is memcpy, not zlib/zstd/lz4/brotli/xz; no side-by-side run against plain zstd or lz4 on the same data was found. Data is synthetic. The README of the repo carries no numbers. Zstd sum_openmp output in the same folder shows compressed-in-memory summation slower than uncompressed (1582 MB/s vs 11818 MB/s at 1 thread). Blosc2 blog and Blosc2-Debunking-Myths.pdf (blosc.org) and the SciPy NDim paper were blocked here; PyPI-snippet figures (memcpy 8.93 GB/s, lz4+shuffle 29.69 GB/s compress) were not verified on a fetched page.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/Blosc/c-blosc2 then bench/results-corex via github.com; WebSearch 'Blosc2 compression faster than memcpy benchmark'

name: libzbitmap
baseline: lzfse (Apple LZBITMAP reference implementation, not open source)
workload: None: the README gives no benchmark; it only states the reimplementation is slower than Apple's original with similar ratios.
claimed_speedup: None. README: 'For now it's much slower than the original, but the ratios obtained are similar.'
tradeoffs: Black-box reverse-engineered reimplementation of Apple LZBITMAP; open source path to decode/encode APFS-style data. Not a speed play.
caveats: No numeric comparison against lzfse, lz4 or any listed baseline; the repo itself says it is slower than Apple's original. lzfse issue #62 (opened) only asks Apple to open source LZBITMAP and has no numbers. Kept as tier D for completeness; likely not faster than any baseline.

name: PISA (Performant Indexes and Search for Academia)
baseline: StreamVByte / SIMD-BP128 (FastPFor) codecs inside the same engine
workload: README cites an ECIR 2019 study: top-10 and top-1000 query latency on a 50-million-document web collection; no per-codec decode-speed table in the repo.
claimed_speedup: No codec-versus-baseline speedup in the repo. README only says average latency 10-40 ms (top 10) and 20-50 ms (top 1000) on 50M documents.
stars_or_usage: 1.1k stars; used by IR research papers
tradeoffs: Search engine, not a standalone codec library: codecs (PEF/opt, SIMD-BP128 default, block_interpolative, block_optpfor, QMX, MaskedVByte, StreamVByte) sit behind the inverted-index API; in-memory index only.
caveats: Springer (ECIR 2019 paper), ceur-ws (OSIRRC paper, HTTP 403), pisa-engine.github.io docs and the Tantivy benchmark game were blocked, so the codec comparison tables could not be read. benchmarks/ in the repo has index_perftest.cpp, perftest_interpolative.cpp and scan_perftest.cpp but no published results. osirrc/pisa-docker has effectiveness numbers only. A Tier A or B record needs the ECIR 2019 paper tables (or the repo's benchmark output) from an environment that reaches Springer.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/pisa-engine/pisa README; WebSearch on the ECIR 2019 paper title

name: hybrid-fenwick-tree
baseline: DYNAMIC (dyn::suc_bv dynamic succinct bitvector) per benchmark source; not SDSL or sux
workload: benchmark/rankselect/rank_select.cpp times dynamic rank, select and update on random bitvectors for Fenwick-based Word/Stride structures against DYNAMIC; plots/rankselect/data/*.csv hold per-size timings.
claimed_speedup: None stated in README. The CSV files (rank1, select1, update, bitspace) hold only the library's own Fenwick variants (fixed, byte, bit; F and L layouts) with no DYNAMIC or SDSL column.
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++17 -O3 -march=native (from benchmark source header and Makefile); README says tested with GCC 8.2 on x86_64 Linux
tradeoffs: Fixed-size dynamic arrays (mutable, no resize); needs GCC builtins; superseded by the version merged into sux (https://github.com/vigna/sux).
caveats: README says 'now part of sux' and its TODO still lists 'Choose a license', but a LICENSE file with MIT text exists. No numeric comparison against SDSL or sux was found; the compared baseline in code is DYNAMIC. CPU model not stated. The Marchini-Vigna paper (compact Fenwick trees) was not fetched. Record is tier D because no speed numbers were read against a named baseline.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/pacman616/hybrid-fenwick-tree README, benchmark/ and plots/ directories

name: genedex
baseline: rust-bio FM-index (bio large, sampling 32); also fm-index crate and sview-fmindex
workload: Locate of 377 MB of 50-base Illumina read queries in an FM-index of human genome hg38 (suffix array sampling 4, lookup depth 10), best of 5 runs, plus index construction time and memory; single-threaded search loop.
claimed_speedup: Locate hg38 running time: genedex flat64 1.6 s (7.2 GB index) and cond64 2.6 s (5.2 GB) versus bio large 7.0 s (19.9 GB), bio small 10.2 s (10.2 GB), fm-index multi text 87.9 s (7.3 GB), sview vec128 2.4 s (5.4 GB), sview vec32 2.3 s (6.9 GB). Derived from page data: flat64 about 4.4x faster than bio large and 1.4x faster than sview vec32.
compiler_and_flags: cargo run --release with rustflags -C target-cpu=native (.cargo/config.toml); rustc version not stated
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6348 @ 2.60GHz, 2 sockets x 28 cores, AVX512, 1 TB RAM
tradeoffs: Early-stage API; sampled suffix array; flat64 trades memory (7.2 GB vs 5.2 GB for cond64) for speed; construction uses libsais and rayon (build threads only).
caveats: Benchmark author is the genedex author (bias alert stated in the benchmark README). Baselines are other Rust crates; no run against SDSL (C++) or sux was found, so the listed baseline is not tested. Numbers were read off the bar-chart SVG (Locate-Hg38.svg, rendered locally). AWRY was excluded from the benchmark for segmentation-fault problems. Only DNA/hg38 workload.

name: AWRY
workload: None in this repo: the README has no benchmark. The C original (AvxWindowFmIndex) paper snippet claims 2-4x faster nucleotide exact-match queries than SeqAn3.
claimed_speedup: None for AWRY. README calls it 'fastest in its class' by reference to the C library paper (doi 10.1186/s13015-021-00204-6); search snippet: C version 2-4x faster than SeqAn3 on nucleotides, 2-6x on amino acids (snippet only).
stars_or_usage: 5 stars on UM-Applied-Algorithms-Lab/AWRY; 0 on the traviswheelerlab copy
tradeoffs: Needs AVX2 or ARM Neon; supports DNA, RNA and protein; parallel_count and parallel_locate via rayon.
caveats: Opened both URLs. The traviswheelerlab/AWRY page showed 0 stars and was summarised as a fork; the UM-Applied-Algorithms-Lab/AWRY page (BSD-3-Clause, 283 commits, last commit 2025-01-14) is the active upstream. No AWRY numbers anywhere. The feldroop/rust-fmindex-benchmark README excluded AWRY for segmentation-fault issues and reports 18x peak memory at construction. Paper snippet comes from a WebSearch result (biorxiv/PMC pages not opened) and concerns the C library, not this port.
